subsubtopic: CALL FOR RESIGNATION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House in order to move a motion on an important matter.

December 3, 1980
In view of the laudable objectives pursued by the government to strike an equitable balance between all Canadians at the social and economic levels and thereby preserve national unity, 1 find unacceptable the attitude taken by the official opposition, especially its leader, who are encouraging divisiveness by constantly speaking, both inside and outside the House, of "a feeling of alienation", "growing separatism", "western frustration" and God knows what else. Such statements do not foster good will and unity in this country.
Since such conduct by a so-called national party and by its leader is totally opposed to the basic philosophy which we should all share, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant):
That the House demand the immediate resignation of the Leader of the Official Opposition because of this conduct which is unsuitable for a true Canadian.

subsubtopic: MORTGAGE GUARANTEES FOR HOMES ON INDIAN RESERVES- MOTION UNDER S. O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that there is a need to improve the quality and quantity of housing on Indian reserves in Canada, that the federal government is the custodian of all reserve lands in Canada, and that direct capital allocation by the federal government for native housing is constantly inadequate, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and/or the federal government provide mortgage guarantees on homes and infrastructure on Indian reserves in order to allow the provincial governments and the private sector to provide the mortgage financing which would enable the private sector to undertake directly the construction of homes under band council direction and supervision, thereby relieving the federal government of the responsibility for some of the capital costs. This type of action by the federal government would support and accelerate the process of self-reliance by the native people of Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I am sure he will not be surprised to learn that my questions relate to what has been Canada's most prominent and heretofore most successful theatre, Stratford's Shakespearean Festival. 1 refer particularly to the minister's recent decision with regard to an application for a work permit for an artistic director. Nor do I think the minister will be surprised to know that I made a
Oral Questions
commitment some weeks ago to conflicting groups not to raise this, particularly as a partisan issue, because it did not appear to me at that time to be in either the interests of the festival or in the national interest to do so.
Having been released from that commitment 1 now ask the minister of immigration whether he intends to publish definitive guidelines with which internationally renowned artistes, directors, producers and so on will have to comply before coming to Canada. I specifically ask for these guidelines because I say with regret that under the present apparent policy even William Shakespeare himself would not be allowed into this country to produce one of his own plays.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the hon. member for his assistance in the past. We have had several interesting conversations about the situation at Stratford and I want to express my appreciation for the many helpful words of advice he has provided.
I do want to suggest to him that his question is phrased in the wrong way. It is not a question of which guidelines apply to international directors; the question is which guidelines apply to companies, groups or organizations in Canada in terms of their hiring policy. As the hon. member well knows, the Immigration Act very clearly states that the primary objective is to ensure that Canadians have first opportunity at any positions which are available in this country. There is a responsibility on the part of any employer to ensure that proper and extensive searches are made to make sure that Canadians do have that opportunity of access to those jobs.
My decision was made purely on the ground that the board of directors of the Stratford Festival had not conducted their search in a way which would make that position available to qualified Canadians. I have no interest in keeping out qualified people, but I do have a responsibility under my ministry to ensure that qualified Canadians at least have a chance at those jobs.

So in effect, the people concerned can benefit from the provisions of the bill which unfortunately has not yet been passed by the House.
Privilege-Mr. Parker
At the time 1 knew the information was incorrect because 1 had copies of writs issued under the provisions of the Railway Act to four of my constituents. So, knowing it was incorrect, 1 gave the minister yet another opportunity to correct the record. On Wednesday, November 26, I offered him exactly that option. His answer was the following:
I have told the House, however, that Foothills had indicated that, as far as compensation is concerned. Foothills is ready to work out compensation arrangements on the basis of the bill introduced by my colleague, Senator Olson, which has not yet been passed by Parliament. Foothills voluntarily agreed to follow the rules proposed in that particular bill. As far as I can sec. nothing has happened which is contradictory to what I indicated to the House or what Foothills had indicated publicly before.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thought that 1 could use the opportunity given to me, that is, the consideration of my departmental expenditures to mention some progress made in the transport area, more especially some achievements in which I have been involved since my appointment to Transport Canada in March last. My speech will be deliberately and openly optimistic because I feel that once in a while one should point out what is going well especially in a country like ours where we tend, too easily perhaps, to be pessimistic. Besides, one can be optimistic without being complacent, smug and self-satisfied. I shall have to recognize, in the next two days, that many things still have to be done, which we will do. The beauty of Canada is that most of its problems can be solved, or at least I think they can.
Mr. Chairman, I hesitated before deciding whether I would present my few observations by mode of transport, that is, air, sea, or land, or else, by area, that is the west, the east and the centre. I opted for the latter, but I shall often have to switch from one to the other. I trust I shall be forgiven for doing so.
Supply

Let us look first at what is happening in western Canada. Economic growth in that region has been greater than in the rest of the country as a whole since 1971. This trend is expected to continue throughout the 1980s. Of course, it will have major implications on the transportation system. The federal government is resolved that the transportation capacity in western Canada will be equal to increasing traffic demands.
Let me give some illustrations of that determination. I would like to recognize once and for all the work which has been done by my predecessors and by other members of this House. It is sometimes advantageous to be at the end of a story, rather than at the beginning, which will be the case in some of the instances I will mention. I say that so that 1 will not have to repeat it too often as I go along.

subsubtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 2, 1980-81
speechtext: You're trying to get us off our guard.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 2, 1980-81
speechtext:
I am trying to butter you up. The first subject is ports on the west coast. Last summer three major issues were resolved. Hon. members will remember that the Roberts Bank port development had been held up because of a federal-provincial dispute over ownership of the bed of Georgia Strait. The agreement was signed in August by the Hon. Don Phillips, representing the government of British Columbia, and myself on behalf of the federal government. Under this agreement the province provides for the transfer of land and water lots to the National Harbours Board without prejudice to the final resolution of legal ownership. This allows the National Harbours Board to proceed with the development of three additional terminal facilities. An amount of $47 million has been allocated to the project by the port of Vancouver, of which Roberts Bank is an integral part. By 1985, an estimated 25 million tons of coal will be shipped from Roberts Bank annually, compared to the present shipments of I I million odd tons.
The second accomplishment which I would like to underline is the project taking place at Ridley Island at Prince Rupert. On the grain side, in line with the memorandum of understanding signed by my predecessor in July, 1979, agreement was reached with the grain consortium last September. Three or four contracts for ground preparations have already been allocated and work has begun. The federal contribution to this part will be approximately $22 million. As everybody knows, a grain elevator worth about $200 million and a dock worth $12 million to $14 million will be constructed by the consortium of grain pools and grain companies.
On the coal side, negotiations are now in their final stages with the Japanese. Perhaps I should not say that, because negotiations such as these can have temporary interruptions. I understand that things may not be concluded. At any rate, the federal government has committed itself to $3 per ton rate at the port which, as far as one can determine at this time, would be equivalent to a grant of some $ 15 million to $20 million.
The third piece of good news is in relation to Duke Point at Nanaimo. Last August 1 had the pleasure of signing another agreement with the B.C. government and the Nanaimo Harbour Board, committing $6 million to this $21 million project

December 3, 1980
Supply
which will make Duke Point the major lumber port on the west coast.
I must mention in all this good news, another agreement, which has not received too much attention in the press and which I signed, also in August, with the hon. Mr. Fraser for the government of British Columbia, dealing with a joint marine terminal study to determine what facilities will be needed on the west coast to the year 2000. This agreement should be an important instrument in policy formulation in the coming years.
The major remaining port problem on the west coast has to do with the status of the port of Vancouver. For a number of years now the Vancouver port community has requested more autonomy in the management of its business. During the last election, the Prime Minister made a positive commitment to that effect. The subject is also of interest to many other ports, if not all of them, under the authority of the National Harbours Board.
As my hon. friends know, this subject of port management has been the object of three bills in the last five years. The debate has been going on for a decade. Bill C-50, which was the last incarnation of that debate in the House of Commons, was not generally supported.
1 have had many meetings throughout the summer with members of the Vancouver Port Authority and other port authorities. Together with my distinguished marine administrator, we looked at the whole issue. As a result of these meetings, the marine administrator has now prepared a position paper in consultation with port authorities. This paper is almost ready for presentation to the cabinet committee. I can indicate the general lines of that position paper. They are very practical ones. We recognize the different categories of ports, although most of the attention goes to the National Harbours Board Act. The idea will be to develop two types of ports and to establish a relationship between the two. In the internal jargon, we call them "mini" and "maxi" corporations. The Harbour Commissions Act of 1964 would not be changed in any substantial fashion.
The legislation will be practical. As 1 understand it, this is in keeping with what interested parties involved in port administration want, as well as the people of Canada.
With respect to grain handling and transportation in western Canada, 1 have made a couple of speeches recently on that subject.
The Canadian Wheat Board says that annual grain exports could grow by 50 per cent by 1985, and farmers have accepted this challenge. The Canadian government has accepted the challenge of providing the best transportation facilities. As everyone knows, the government record is pretty good if one considers that in the last decade it has invested a sum of about $1.3 billion in improving the western rail transportation system, although 1 might add that the hon. member for Medicine Hat, others and myself, say that it is still not good enough yet.

There is still a lot to be done even when one admits that quite a lot has been accomplished in the last decade.
To correct this situation, that is, make the system as good as it should and could be, most people agree that there are two major areas to tackle. One is the upgrading of the railway facilities. The other is the modernization of the Crowsnest Pass freight rate. It is possible that my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for St. Boniface, will want to say more about that. However, I will be in a position, I hope, in the upcoming discussion to answer most of the questions as to what is taking place now by way of branch line rehabilitation, boxcar rehabilitation, branch line subsidies, the grain transportation co-ordinator, and so on.
During the summer I had the good fortune to see CN and CP equipment in the mountain region. At the time federal and provincial ministers saw new signalling equipment, new tracks being laid by extremely modern means, hot box detectors linked with electronic equipment. It was very impressive. I think CN and CP are now quite proud to show the progress which has been made.
1 will not repeat speeches I have made about the Crowsnest. I will just say that more and more people agree that some change must take place. On November 15, 1979, my predecessor, the hon. member for Vegreville said the following as reported in Hansard at page 1359:
Not everyone agrees with the solutions and not everyone agrees with the diagnosis of the problems that are before us.
He went on to say:
there are different views as to how we might best turn the system around.
Partly through his efforts, and partly through the efforts of the previous minister of transport, and also through the efforts of a number of leaders in that industry in western Canada, I think one can say that the consensus on the need to modernize has grown substantially in the last year. On December 1, 1980, the hon. member for Medicine Hat was saying just about the same thing. As reported in Hansard at page 5219, he said:
There are many farmers in western Canada who do not completely understand what is behind the Crowsnest Pass freight rate and what it does-
And I want to emphasize the words "and what it does". The hon. member went on to say:
to the total agricultural economy and the total Canadian economy.
Many other people and 1 have been saying that, and 1 just want to associate a westerner with an easterner in saying those things, to strengthen my credibility on the matter.
In any event, I spent a lot of time, not as much as I would have liked to last week in Calgary and the week before in Regina, discussing those matters with leaders in the industry and farmers. I have been trying to express my great desire about contributing to the modernization of the western grain handling and transportation system.
There is a passage in the budget speech concerning the Western Development Fund which attracted the attention of a
December 3, 1980

lot of members when it was read by the Minister of Finance. Like everyone else, 1 hope this fund can be helpful in solving or improving upon the Crowsnest situation at this time.
Both inside the department and outside we have worked hard on this subject. We have produced a position paper which is in the decison-making pipeline. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat has promised his support in advance, in due course I will be looking for the support of all members on all sides of the House on the initiatives which will be taken.
I would like to mention something else concerning western Canada. It has to do with the bilateral air agreement with the United Kingdom, signed in September last. A number of people wrote telling me how important this bilateral agreement was to western Canada in its air relationship with Europe, in particular, and also in its air relationship with the Far East, by way of Vancouver and Hong Kong. When this agreement was signed, unfortunately not too many people wrote to say they were pleased. However, I guess that is the story of our lives. It is good news to me, and I hope that my western friends share in that sentiment.
There is also the search and rescue program which is of interest to western Canada. The opposition increased the budget last year when they were in government. We have gone further this year for next year. The coast guard base was opened during the summer and four new ships have been assigned to the west coast.
I would have liked to have talked about the CN rail relocation in Regina and the multimodal station. I presume my friends will raise some of these subjects.
With respect to central Canada, I am very much aware of the preoccupation of some members regarding the lack of visible progress on a number of very ticklish issues. 1 refer to the sale of Nordair to the private sector, the transfer of air routes from Dorval to Mirabel, the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal STOL project. All of these are very difficult problems. In my view progress is being made, particularly in the last mentioned one. I hope to be in Toronto in the coming days to meet with all interested parties, and that further progress will be accomplished.
I have more good news. The seaway made a profit for the first time. The port of Thunder Bay is thriving. The port of Montreal is doing very well. A decision on a third terminal at Malton will be made soon. The first steps have been taken on the expansion of the Hamilton airport, etc., etc., etc., as the Minister of Agriculture would say.
I would like to single out two progress areas, one being VIA Rail and the other the coming agreement with Quebec on Montreal urban transit.
VIA is a great challenge. There is no doubt about that. As my note says, it is nothing less than a reversal of historic trends of declining clientele, of increasing operating deficits, of deteriorating facilities and equipment. It is a great challenge, but again progress is being made. It is not at the speed at
Supply
which the hon. member for Regina West would like, but nevertheless it is progress.
Mr. Roberts, the president of VIA, said that the number of passengers was up by 41 per cent since 1976. The load factor this year to date has been 50 per cent compared to 35 per cent when passenger transportation was handled by the railway companies. One way of looking at the progress of VIA is that they are not losing as much money as the railways say they would have lost had they continued to operate the passenger service.
A number of new initiatives are currently being undertaken.
I can only tick off what they are: first, a major capital investment program to refurbish old equipment and replace it, as necessary, with new equipment. Hon. members know about the purchase of S90 million worth of Light, Rapid and Comfortable equipment. There is the computerized reservation system, Reservia, introduced in April, 1980. This has been an improvement. In its first days I received a tremendous amount of mail, as 1 am sure other members did. The fact that 1 no longer get any is a clear indication of an improvement. It is better than a Gallup poll.

Mr. Chairman, 1 am sure the minister will have ample time to conclude his remarks throughout the course of today and tomorrow. 1 thank him for his summary. I note his degree of optimism in his review of progress that has been made. I suppose I could make the comment that in his review he merely recapped a number of the initiatives that had been started. What has transpired over the last nine months is essentially a recycling of a number of programs, perhaps dressed up in Liberal wrapping and Liberal press releases, especially when he suggests that Prince Rupert and Roberts Bank are great achievements. I am sure everyone knows those projects were well under way to being concluded at the time the minister took over this office.
The minister talked about the desire and the necessity of increasing transportation capacity in western Canada. I thought he would seize upon that opportunity to outline some new initiatives on how that would be achieved. He merely mentioned it in passing, and went back to reviewing some of the projects that have been before us for some time. I am rather disappointed that the minister did not come forward today and announce some new initiatives which we would welcome. Perhaps, if they were substantive, we might even conclude this debate earlier than originally anticipated.

The minister talked about grain, and here again he reviewed the past. He did not announce anything for the future in terms of what may be done with respect to the port of Churchill. I sense that that port is no longer a priority. As a matter of fact, we were told that the MV Arctic was going to return to Churchill some time in the month of November.

I am not sure whether it is going to come in January, or later on in December. I hope that Churchill is still a very important component in the movement of grain for export.
Reference was also made to the fact that a paper has been prepared on the statutory freight rate. Naturally, we will await that with interest. It will no doubt be the subject of some very interesting debate. I hope that members of Parliament, and hopefully the committee, will have an opportunity to examine in detail some of the options and the direction in which he intends to move.
Our party chose the subject of transportation for the express purpose of reviewing progress or lack of progress in a number of areas. It is a very important element in this country. We sense that because of the government's preoccupation with constitutional and energy matters, some of the very basic bread and butter issues related to transportation have been relegated to the back burner. The government has now been in office for some nine months. I think I am fair in saying we regret very much the lack of progress and of any new initiatives being undertaken by this administration and this minister.
I am going to raise a couple of points. Hopefully the minister can respond. My colleagues will be opening up a number of other areas. The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East will be dealing primarily with marine issues, an area in which he has long held a very attentive interest that has contributed very much to the development of policy in this country.
I want to deal first with rail passenger policy. 1 am pleased that the minister included VIA Rail in his remarks. We had the good fortune of having Mr. Roberts, the president of VIA Rail, before our committee in the past week or so. 1 think all members of the committee were pleased with his enthusiasm, notwithstanding the very difficult job and the challenges which he faces. However, there are some areas which require government attention and some improvement.
The president of VIA Rail, Mr. Roberts, pointed out the difficulty that VIA Rail is having with respect to the open-endedness of the contracts that have been signed with the two respective railroads and the fact that there was an additional $30 million supplementary estimate which now increases the subsidy toward rail passenger service to the amount of some $455 million. He indicated it was because of additional charges that were levied by the railways, notwithstanding the fact that a contract had been entered into.
The contract that is in existence is open-ended so that the railways can come back a year or so later and bill VIA for additional charges. That makes it very difficult in terms of planning and in terms of route structure and cash flow. Naturally, VIA Rail has filed a dispute with the CTC. Because of the lack of disclosure of cost information data they must rely upon others, so the matter has been referred to the CTC. If we look at past history, it will not be dealt with for perhaps two or three years. That makes it very difficult in terms of their being able to plan ahead.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister will agree with me there has to be some move towards a fixed price contract for at least a 12-month period. That has to be put in place. While the minister may not be directly involved, I would hope that he would provide the necessary moral support to VIA Rail in order that that might be achieved.
Notwithstanding the fact that this element does create difficulty in long-term planning, we asked the president of VIA Rail to provide the committee with a five-year plan and submit it to the committee so that we could look at it, analyse it, and ask some questions on it. In doing this it would give us some indication of where VIA Rail intends to move over the next five-year period. The president indicated he was unable to provide a five-year detailed plan. He said:
There is a cabinet document that has been put together by Transport Canada that will be going to cabinet in the near future, and that will show what is contained in our five-year plan, and when that is approved then we will have we want to make sure that five-year becomes a public document so everybody knows exactly where we are going.
The fact of the matter is, according to Mr. Roberts, that Via Rail is unable to provide the minister and indeed the committee with a five-year plan because there is no long-term policy developed. I know from past experience that much has been done in terms of developing a long-term rail passenger policy. There has been a tremendous amount of detailed and background work done by Transport Canada officials. Unless there have been some dramatic shifts, or unless there is a dramatic alteration in government policy, it would seem to me that it would be only sensible that this discussion paper and formulation of a cabinet document which was put in place during the time of our administration in December, 1979, should be moved forward. Perhaps there are some details that should be changed. I find it very disturbing that this has been neglected and not proceeded with.
I should like to ask the minister, given the fact that he has had access to the discussion papers, the background information, and the very comprehensive analysis provided by his officials, why the delay? Why the foot-dragging? Why do we not have a comprehensive rail passenger policy so that VIA can conform to that policy and we can have some long-term planning?
It seems to me that it is the only sensible way to go and thereby eliminate some of the ad hocery that takes place. Can the minister answer that question and, at the same time, give some indication to us of what his initial reaction is to the recent study that has been provided for Transport Canada by the Canadian Institute of Guided Ground Transport, Queen's
December 3, 1980

University? It seems to me this is a forward-looking document which may very well provide the impetus for some revolutionary changes in terms of our transportation industry, and particularly with respect to rail passenger service in terms of rationalizing all modes of transportation. I hope that the minister might answer those two or three questions without utilizing the balance of my 20 minutes so that I may get on to a couple of other subjects.

On Churchill my hon. friend would love to know,
I am sure, that the MV Arctic has been there last month to pick up 25,000 tons of wheat for Italy. I tried to provoke a question in the House at the time but 1 could not get anybody to ask it. It is good news, and the opposition is not normally as interested in that as in the bad news.
On the subject of the Crow modernization, I recognize that 1 talked mostly about the paper now in front of cabinet committee. In my recent speeches in the west I went further than that and did say a number of things about the spirit of the exercise we had been conducting during the summer and about the procedure that will be followed. I happen to believe that a negotiating commission would be helpful. There is common ground between the western agricultural conference and the commodity coalition-a number of common elements-but my view is that it would be very useful if this, as I said in Regina, were "massaged" further and carried as far as possible. Then the government would state its position on the modernization of the Crow. I can see very well that the transportation committee will want to give the bill, when it comes, a lot of attention.
As far as the railway-VIA pricing agreements are concerned, indeed one cannot be too satisfied with the system that exists now. I have referred to it as the Japanese thirteenth month, that is, the possibility of adding to the 12 payments. VIA is charged by CN and CP on the basis of the famous costing order R6313. As my hon. friend said, it is slightly open-ended. The current contract between CP, CN and VIA is in the process of being renegotiated. VIA hopes very much to improve the situation when a new agreement takes place next April, and my department and myself will certainly support the interest of VIA in this matter.
The five-year plan was prepared by VIA in the framework of its capital budget. The five-year plan is being reviewed now. It has been reviewed by the department, of course, and will be reviewed by cabinet in January as part of the long-term options on VIA. 1 hope to share with hon. members that review once the cabinet has expressed its own beliefs on the matter. In considering all this, my hon. friend, others and I should be conscious of the fact that VIA has really been moving for only two years, so we are still at the origin of this transformation, and consequently I do not feel uneasy about not having talked in clearcut terms about the VIA experience and about where VIA will be going from now on. In other words, the phenomenon is still quite new.

Mr. Chairman, given the urgency of developing new public forms of transportation, particularly in the rail passenger sector, as a result of the energy crisis and a number of other influences which have come about since the adoption of VIA, 1 wonder if the minister would not consider it of paramount importance that a long-term strategy be developed and clearcut government policy be developed.
I know from experience that a lot of work has gone into that, and 1 think it would really benefit this House and Canadians at large to hear a clearcut statement of government policy with respect to the future of rail passenger service, the rationalization, what particular area it will be deemed to serve the best, and where we might be able to rationalize and develop a truly integrated intermodal system in this country because, in my view, that happens to be the best way to approach this whole subject. I urge that the minister indeed reconsider the importance of the adoption of a long-term policy so that we can have it and judge the performance of the minister and of the government commensurate with that staled policy.
1 hope the minister will also respond with respect to urban transportation policy. Here again we have an absence of a comprehensive and clearcut urban transportation policy, which is something which has been lacking for many years. The whole approach to urban transportation seems to be based on ad hoc decisions rather than on any global approach.
I know that there has been a very comprehensive document prepared by the minister's officials which clearly sets the stage for the evolution or development of a comprehensive urban transportation policy. The document sets out the current setting, provides alternatives, discusses those alternatives, and sets out the various implications and the effects they might have. I would like to ask the minister whether this work has been ignored. Is it being utilized? Has it been scrapped? Is it being upgraded? In short, what is happening?
When we look at the budget and the energy policy, we really do not see any clear indication from the government with respect to providing any funding for the encouragement of new forms of public transportation, particularly surface public transportation both in urban centres and intercity. I wonder why there has not been any advancement in that area as well. I know there have been negotiations over the years with the province of Ontario, the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec in relation to some rather comprehensive schemes for urban transportation.
It seems to me that the time has come for us to deal with this in terms of establishing an over-ail urban transportation framework. We recognized this when we were in office and attempted to work toward not only the establishment of a comprehensive policy, but also within the framework of that

speechtext:
1 want to raise a matter which I am sure will generate some sympathy and agreement from the minister and from the hon. member for Vegreville, who was the previous minister. Besides the Minister of Transport, the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance should really also be sitting here. Whether I or anyone else agrees with the programs, commitments and policies of the present minister, his predecessor and the one before, is not the point; they are repeatedly turned down by the cabinet or the Treasury Board on the ground of what I still call the mindless Proposition 13 syndrome about too much government, cutting back and reducing expenditures. The programs which are still waiting to be implemented would not be expenditures. They would be investments, and the return on those investments to the Canadian economy and to provincial, municipal and federal governments would more than recover the costs.
I have listened to this minister and four of his predecessors since 1 came here, and 1 must say that I give this minister first place for announcing the things he will look into and is still looking into. Questions are asked by me and by other members, including some on the minister's own side of the House. He is going to look into a number of things, including the Crow rate. He is still doing that. There never has been any argument that a change in the system has to be made. The argument is only about how the change should be made, not that a change should be made. That is agreed to by everyone in the country.
The minister and his two predecessors refused to listen to a commission appointed by his government several years ago. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall made a definitive analysis, the best ever done before or since. If the minister would just implement Mr. Justice Hall's recommendations there would be no fight left out in western Canada regarding the Crow rate. However, the minister is still looking into it.
The minister is the greatest looking-into minister I have ever known. He is going to look into the airport issues in Toronto. They are still being looked into, yea, these many years. He will
look into the number of safety inspectors. That is still being looked into. He will look into the question of asbestos tailings being used in ballast on railway lines. That is still being looked into. He will look into short takeoff and landing. That is still being looked into. It has been looked into for 11 years. He will look into rail line relocation, airport terminals, multimodal transportation centres. These have been looked into until hell won't have it.
The minister and his predecessors say they agree that they want to do a certain thing, they make announcements and commitments and come to agreements with provincial governments and municipalities, but when it comes to getting the money put on the barrelhead for federal participation, the provincial governments and municipalities are turned down. Then they come back to the House of Commons or they go out to the people with whom they made agreements, or to whom they made commitments, and say, "Well, the Treasury Board has turned us down," as though they were helpless.
I want to suggest to the Minister of Transport that in view of the number of things he wants to do, with some of which 1 and other hon. members agree, it is about time he went to the Treasury Board and said, "Look, this is our government's policy. This is the commitment we made, these are the agreements we signed. You will either put up the money or I quit." It is about time that he had some guts in dealing with the people in his own outfit. This does not just apply to this minister; it applies to several others. We have had four successive announcements and press conferences in Regina, from three ministers of transport, about rail line relocation and commitments and agreements on cost-sharing.
I should like the minister to make note of one question which I shall put to him, and I hope I will leave him some time to answer it. If not, I will send him a letter. Is it true that Saskatchewan has agreed to use $3 million of the funds allocated to that province under UTAP, which is really supposed to be for grade separations, and the whole $9 million is supposed to be spread around the whole province? Is it true that Saskatchewan has agreed to use $3 million of the $9 million for phase I of the Regina rail line relocation? If it is true, then when the hell will he get the other $40 million out of Treasury Board? We must get started on it. We have been waiting four years and a host of other things have been held up. It is a commitment and a promise of government policy. When in God's name will he do it?
The minister mentioned that he would deal with issues on a regional basis. Since I only have a few minutes left and my colleagues will be raising numerous items in this discussion, I should like to raise a couple of other matters. The minister spoke about the sale of Nordair. Let me remind the minister that Air Canada had no choice. In fact they were given two choices: it was either compulsory or they had to do it. When PWA and Transair were provided with prairie routes into Winnipeg and in the prairies. Air Canada had to give up $12
December 3, 1980

million worth of passenger revenue and two flights a day in and out of Regina and Saskatoon, and Edmonton-Calgary.
Air Canada was replaced by Pacific Western and, according to the agreement, in exchange the $12 million would be picked up by Nordair flights between Winnipeg and Toronto. If the minister approves the sale of Nordair, the whole $12 million of lost revenue given up by Air Canada will go down the drain. This is damn strange when it comes to developing a regional air policy under the so-called private enterprise competition theory. After Air Canada has built up its routes with the taxpayers' money, as soon as it starts making money, here come the free enterprisers. Where the hell were they when we needed them? The money-paying routes are taken away from Air Canada, which prevents it from providing reasonable service to people in isolated parts of Canada where they lose money. As a result there is a reduction of services in small and medium-sized cities and in the isolated parts of Canada. Surely that requires a fundamental change in the air policy of this country, and I hope the minister will comment on that.
The minister has mentioned VIA Rail. It did not have a good beginning with all the handicaps which plagued it at the start. It was started in exactly the same way as Canadian National was in 1923. It has a debt load which it will not live long enough to pay off unless a subsequent Parliament, years from now, writes it off or transfers it into shares. VIA Rail was stuck for $70 million in equipment from CN and CP which it should have had for $1 a car. Both CN and CP received great benefits in tax write-offs and depreciation. For that equipment they did not deserve more than $1 a car. That is the kind of thing with which VIA Rail started off. It will be held up as a terrible example of a rail passenger service which does not work, or of a corporation that is no good. If you started off in that kind of situation, what the devil can you expect? I am amazed at the good job they are doing, given the circumstances and the framework under which they have to work.
The operating agreement between VIA Rail and CN-CP is one in which the minister and the Canadian Transport Commission have to intervene. They must make available to VIA Rail the unit cost which CN and CP use. VIA Rail does not have a clue as to what the devil it is paying for. It does not know how much it is being charged for the use of a railway station, hot water, steam, or whatever. All this information is kept confidential by the railroads. It was turned over to the Canadian Transport Commission and to the minister, but they will not turn it over to VIA Rail, and VIA Rail has to negotiate an operating agreement blind. Surely that must stop.
When it comes to operating trains in Canada, the kind of operating priority that CN and CP can give to a unit coal train, unit grain train or any kind of unit freight train, is amazing. The minister and the CTC have to require both CN and CP to give the same kind of priority to a unit passenger train. We should be able to move people in this country as fast as we can move pigs.
On the matter of STOL, Mr. Chairman, this is an elitist, bourgeois operation for deputy ministers, business executives,
Supply
and members of Parliament to fly between Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal. That is not what we need from short takeoff and landing aircraft. We need them on our east and west coasts, we need them in the north in the territories, and we need them in the northern parts of our provinces where it is not necessary to build big airports and where all the little isolated communities can be provided with a decent service. You can land and take off on a gravel strip or a beach, if you have to. That is where you put STOL aircraft. We can say to the workers and to the manufacturer, "We will need more of STOL aircraft for that purpose than we would for some elitist service out of Toronto Island." It is a total waste and total duplication.
Perhaps the minister would care to read the study which he commissioned from the Canadian Institute of Ground Transportation. We need a fundamental change in policy. We need people in the Department of Transport who do not have propellers or jet engines for brains. We can move people from Toronto to Ottawa and to Montreal in that triangle, let alone to Quebec and Windsor, at speeds of up to 160 miles an hour and at a cost recovery price of $22 a person, versus $55 cost recovery per passenger, on average of conventional air travel and STOL. That $55 cost per passenger does not include airport costs; those are still handled by the taxpayers.
This nation must develop something that all of Europe, Japan, Australia and New Zealand have done, that is, the electrification of the urban transit system and railway lines. The Soviet Union has electrified 100,000 kilometres of railway track in the last 25 years. If you were to electrify 10,000 miles of lines in Canada, that is just 20 per cent of our trackage, to handle 75 per cent of our freight and passenger traffic-1 wish the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources were here-the amount of diesel fuel saved in one year wouid be enough to seed and harvest many crops in the three prairie provinces. We are up to here in electricity and we will have a surplus of it. We will start exporting even more electricity to the United States. It is not a case of just the production of energy; it is making better use of our energy resources. We can be electrifying urban transit systems.
As I say, we can electrify 20 per cent of our main rail lines, and if they transfer just 20 per cent of the increasing volume of traffic from air and road to electrified rail, the amount of diesel fuel saved would be enough to seed and harvest 12 prairie crops in one year; it would be enough to run all interprovincial buses in Canada for 25 years; it would be enough to heat hundreds of thousands of Canadian homes, the ones stuck with heating oil because natural gas was unavailable to them. Surely this is a sensible and rational way in which to reorganize the transportation system. It requires a fundamental change in present and past government policy.
I will sit down in a minute and let the minister reply in whatever time 1 have left, but I want to assure him that if 1 and my colleagues have another chance to raise this matter and other items today and tomorrow, we will do so. We will

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to be able to speak after people as knowledgeable in the area of transport as the Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Vegreville and the hon. member for Regina West. I particularly appreciated the comments of the minister because he gaves us a list of all that is going on in the Department of Transport. Unfortunately, he was not allowed to complete his remarks.
However, I agree with the hon. member for Vegreville that, in the nine months we have been in power, the Department of Transport has not had such a high profile as it should have had and as the hon. member and myself might have wished. This is because our government has dealt mostly with the constitutional and energy policies. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, the Standing Committee on Transport, under the able leadership of the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), has been one of our most active committees and has heard a great many witnesses. Because of this, all members of the House have been able to participate and to understand fully the decisions that the government must now make in Canada.
During the 20 minutes allotted to me this afternoon, I would like to concentrate strictly on air transport, and especially on two aspects of this means of transport: First the absence of policy concerning regional carriers, and second, the Nordair file. The minister said that he had nearly completed or was about to present to the cabinet a policy paper on second level carriers, and I am happy about this because the present situation in Canada is quite impossible.
December 3, 1980

The most recent policy concerning second level carriers goes back more than ten years. This was when Don Jamieson was transport minister and at the time he had divided Canada in five regions. Since then, the Canadian Transport Commission has had to make several rulings on this policy, and because this is provided in the legislation, several of these judgments had been appealed to cabinet. In fact, Mr. Chairman, cabinet recently reversed the ruling of the Canadian Transport Commission concerning an application and a decision of the commission involving CP Air and Eastern Provincial Airways. CP Air had applied for permission to go as far as Elalifax and Eastern Provincial Airways for permission to go to Toronto.
Without passing judgment on whether or not the decision of the cabinet or the Canadian Transport Commission is justified, it is now obvious that any regional carrier application to the CTC for any route whatsoever in Canada is now useless, except to get a decision that will be appealed, because the policy, which in fact no longer exists, unfortunately, is such a mishmash that I wonder sincerely what the commission will do in a few weeks when it studies the application of Quebecair for landing rights in Toronto. If we go back to the policy of Mr. Jamieson, we realize that granting Quebecair access to that area, that is, to Toronto, would be contrary to that policy. And if it is in fact contrary to that policy, then the CTC should say no. So, considering the irregularities or weaknesses in the policy as it now applies, the ruling of the CTC is absolutely useless because a final decision will come from cabinet which, once again, on an ad hoc basis will indicate to the Canadian people what its policy is with regard to regional carriers.
Mr. Chairman, I am happy to see that the minister is about to submit a policy to cabinet because the examples I have just given really prove the dangers of a lack of policy, for which I do not blame him because he inherited it, but still, a lack of policy just the same. I feel it is imperative for the CTC to have, the sooner the better, specific instructions so that all Canadians and all carriers who need permits, who need routes, can go before the commission knowing that it has a policy to apply, and how cabinet will react under normal circumstances.
I should now like to deal with the Nordair file. When one is a member of Parliament the best way to make headlines is to say that the government is trying to put one over the province you represent. The best way to make sure that you will be seen on television in the evening is to attack the government. The best way for the hon. member for Joliette to make the headlines in the evening is to state, in his unique style, that Quebec is being conned. And that is what they say about the Nordair file. Furthermore, 1 would have liked the former transport minister, the hon. member for Vegreville, in the few minutes he had, to tell hon. members of the Elouse what was the solution he put forward in the Nordair file because, as we know, he was about to submit such a solution to cabinet, and according to what I heard in the department, I tend to believe, Mr. Chair-
Supply
man, that the hon. member for Joliette perhaps would not have been pleased with the decision of the hon. member for Vegreville when he was minister of transport.
I would have liked him to tell us that but, of course, he did not say a word about his policy on Nordair. The hon. member for Joliette has told me that he intends to participate in the debate tomorrow. Therefore, I am looking forward to hearing what he is going to tell us, and 1 also hope that he is going to repeat that at the Progressive Conservative caucus when they meet, because 1 agree with him.
The last thing 1 want to see happening is for Quebec to be gypped and I am convinced that such is not the case but I would not feel so certain if the former government were still in power. Mr. Chairman, let us take a closer look at this file as it is and I do not want to indulge in petty partisanship in this respect. 1 do not want to say that because Nordair is actually located in Montreal all interests in this company should be held by Quebeckers. Perish the thought, Mr. Chairman. However, 1 do say that the minister has been presented with two serious applications, one from the Lizotte group and the other from the Desjardins group. The expertise of these two groups in aeronautics is outstanding; it is a well-acknowledged fact. Both have current expertise in aviation. Therefore one can say that they are both equally qualified. Both groups have attracted various investors, co-op style groups or certain other elements that do not necessarily happen to be located in the province of Quebec.
And it was precisely toward a majority share in the Lizotte or Hamel-also called Desjardins-interests that the department's policy seemed to be directed. Even though the matter seemed to be progressing fairly well, there was a certain uncertainty; both parties wanted a quick decision, they wanted the minister to skip a few steps, but 1 think he was wise in waiting because the situation was not ripe. I agreed with the minister's view. But I became concerned when the newspapers reported that the minister wanted a 40-40-20 division, with 40 per cent of the interests in Ontario, 40 per cent in Quebec and 20 per cent to Air Canada.
I would first like to comment on Air Canada's equity. Basically, I see no problem because in any investment scheme Air Canada would bring a certain wisdom, a financing capacity, and an unquestionable expertise. But in a 40-40-20 scheme, effective control goes to Air Canada, in cases of controversy between the two groups, and I am not sure that I would want to give that power to Air Canada, because, as we all recall, the government policy was to save Nordair by asking Air Canada to purchase it and to sell it off afterwards to the private sector, and that policy, as far as I know, remains unchanged. But if Air Canada retains control by having the number of shares necessary to vote in cases of controversy, then 1 see problems. Without being against Air Canada having equity, I want to make sure that the distribution of Nordair shares would not allow Air Canada to exercise such power.

But I see especially serious problems in the 40-40 Quebec-Ontario split because I do not think that, in air transport specifically, decisions should be based on a geographical map, and that is precisely what the minister's advisers are trying to achieve. The worst thing that could happen to Nordair-and 1 do not dare think that it may happen-would be splitting the company into "Air Ontario" and "Air Quebec". I think that would constitute a major step backwards in Canadian air policy. I realize that some ultra-nationalist groups would like you to do so, but they ignore the basic facts of the air industry in Canada and they serve very short-term and nationalist purposes when advocating a policy which would be prejudicial to Canada, Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the best and most basic aspect of any air policy is that no province is involved and that it has no frontier.
So 1 think the minister ought to avoid a 40-40-20 split. 1 consider that such a distribution is senseless. ITowever, as 1 said earlier, it does not mean that I would remove any minority or majority interest of a few provinces or businessmen within those provinces. Far from it. But an arbitrary 40-40-20 split as suggested would give rise to some serious problems. Is Nordair a Quebec or Ontario carrier? Mr. Chairman, 1 refuse to answer such questions because how can we identify a Quebec or an Ontario company when most of its flights are between Montreal and Ottawa, Montreal and Hamilton, Montreal and Pittsburgh and Toronto and Pittsburgh? What happens then? Is it an Ontario, a Quebec or an American company? It is above all a Canadian company and this is the fact that should not be forgotten. Basically, Nordair must remain under Canadian ownership.
There are now suggestions that most of Nordair's business, the major part of their traffic is not in eastern but central Canada. As far as Nordair is concerned, people who analyse the matter-and 1 am sure the hon. member for Vegreville will agree on this-those who look at the routes realize that the $15 million invested by Nordair in those passenger routes have not been recovered yet and that in effect, in terms of return on dollar investments, its passenger traffic is in the red. It must be realized that Nordair's profitable routes are not the passenger ones but the northern routes serving the Dew line, defence bases, the Inuit and the Indians. That is where Nordair is making its money. For that reason I refuse to identify Nordair in a 40-40-20 per cent split. So there are these two groups, the Desjardins group and the Lizotte group. I suggest we should use an approach along the lines of Solomon's judgment. 1 suggest we take the most favourable aspects of both applications.
Unquestionably, the best element on the Lizotte group side is employee participation. This is something that I, as a member of Parliament, would like to see more often in our Canadian corporations. It could go as far as having one or two employee representatives on Nordair's board of directors. Mr. Lizotte himself does not preclude the possibility, were his group's application to be turned down, of joining forces with the Desjardins group, with employee participation. 1 read this in a report by Claude Beauchamp in the Montreal journal Les affaires. Mr. Andre Lizotte said so in so many words. 1 am not making this up. The best aspect of the Lizotte group being employee participation, let us now apply that to the other group, the Desjardins group. We see that the Desjardins group is made up by Alfred Hamel and the Provost family who are without doubt known in Quebec as the leaders in transportation in that province and whose expertise is established in multimodal transport by road or by air, Mr. Chairman.
As we are clearly dealing with strong personalities, with Mr. Lizotte on one side and Mr. Hamel on the other, the solution would then be to regroup all that under an umbrella which could be the Desjardins Investment Company. Again, the reputation of this financial institution is well established, its vitality is well-known and it is led by respectable Quebeckers one of whom we met recently, Mr. Guy Bernier, the president of that company.
I would therefore suggest that the leadership be given to the Desjardins group which could combine the best aspects of the Lizotte group, employee participation, Alfred Hamel and Mr. Provost. We would then have a very dynamic team. But the reason for a decision must be taken into consideration.
When the government took over Nordair, it was fully aware of the economic problems the regional carriers were facing at that time. Therefore, we must clearly remember that any regional policy in Canada must stem from an attempt at rationalization. We must make sure that both companies are healthy and that our goal is not to cause competition between them but to combine their organizations, and I know you will agree with me on what both Quebec and Canada want, regional carriers in good standing.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to interrupt the minister if he wishes to respond to that eloquent plea, most of which I think we can agree with although I would remind the hon. member that it was the government which caused the problem in the first place. There are many items which will be raised over the course of today and tomorrow while we are on estimates. 1 myself have some 13 points to raise, and I wish that we had twice the length of time that is allotted to deal with the matter. I will touch on my points briefly and then I will narrow in on specific areas with questions to the minister.
I will talk about pending legislation on matters with which we can deal. I would like to discuss the sense of commitment of the minister with respect to the export of our raw resources, specifically, coal on the west coast, and the requirements for imported oil to the west coast. These points will be raised in the context of the commitment which was firmly entered into by the previous government, and by the government prior to that, with respect to the re-establishment of Canada as a cargo shipping or deep-sea shipping nation.
December 3, 1980

In connection with this matter I will deal with the minister's attitude with respect to cargo preference laws, particularly in the bulk trades. I want to know what the minister has done or intends to do about closing the waters north of 60 degrees, including Ungava Bay, Hudson Bay and James Bay. 1 would like to discuss safety at sea and the current emphasis on education. 1 want to discuss the upgrading and expansion of certain of our Canadian coast-guard facilities. I would like to know from the minister the government's direction with respect to our shallow water ice-breaking capabilities, and 1 again want to emphasize my growing concern about unprotected bridge piers in navigable waters in Canada.
1 want to continue the philosophizing which the minister initiated late one afternoon in committee on the propriety of Canadian National investing, through order in council, in Cast Shipping sufficient moneys through the purchase of class A preferred shares to the extent that-1 presume at its will-it can take up the option of full management and control. In that regard 1 will put a specific question to the minister as to whether or not he continues to believe it is proper for Crown corporations such as Canadian National to invest taxpayers' dollars in companies which are essentially foreign owned. For example, Cast Shipping is registered offshore in tax havens. This company does not employ Canadians and, indeed, provides very little residual economic benefit to our country.
Perhaps in another context later on the minister could give some indication as to when the St. Lawrence River will close, and some indication of the anticipated onboard grain storage on the lakes this winter. As I indicated, those are some of the general areas with which I would like to deal.
1 would like to come back to Cast Shipping for a moment. I would like the minister to give the chamber the benefit of his expertise in this area and tell us exactly how much money the government has authorized for investment in that company. Would he tell the House what percentage of the class A preferred shares of that company were purchased by Canadian National? Also, it is my understanding that in some 13 or 14 months Canadian National will have to indicate its intention to the government. I would like to know generally what the minister's attitude is concerning this, specifically, whether or not the government is in agreement.
In today's Globe and Mail we notice that Cast, which is a foreign company, although it is owned by Canadians domiciled in Europe, is moving to acquire the St. Lawrence Stevedoring Co. of Montreal together with major bulk cargo handling facilities at Montreal and Quebec City. Cast uses Canadian tax dollars. Its profits go offshore. Consequently the company is not properly taxed here in Canada. Its ships' crews arc foreign. Therefore, no tax dollars accrue to the Canadian government.
It would seem that Cast, with CN's AAA credit rating is about to run around the country and buy everything up hoping, 1 suppose, to avoid the objections of Canadian National doing this openly and under its own name. By using Cast,
Supply
CN, when it has purchased and taken control of those facilities in its immediate interest, could then exercise its option for class A preferred shares and take over full management and control of that company. As I have said, this is a company whose basic corporate structure lies outside Canada. 1 am somewhat disturbed by it. 1 am a little frustrated that we have not had quite as much openness with respect to this matter as would seem to be appropriate. I would like to know where CN is going and to what degree it intends to use Cast to do things CN otherwise is not prepared to do.
For many years another area of continuing concern to me has been the redevelopment of a Canadian merchant marine. I see distinguished members of the National Harbours Board are with us today. It was not necessarily the age of the Canadian merchant fleet in the late 1940s which caused its demise. It was not necessarily high crew costs. It was not directly "labour" which led to the very drastic reduction in the number of Canadian-owned and registered ships on the oceans of this world. It was not those factors alone. Indeed, the greatest factor was the deliberate decision by government to unload the old Park Steamship Company. With that and the government's deliberate decision-not an accidental one at all-not to lend assistance which would have enabled the private sector to replace that capacity, this contributed, in my opinion, to the loss of Canada's presence on the high seas. At that time Canada's shipping fleet was among the top seven or eight in the world.
Today, while we may have 100 or 120 Canadian-owned ships offshore, they are not registered in Canada. In some cases they carry some Canadian crew but in other cases they carry no Canadian crew. These ships are registered, without exception, in so-called countries of convenience for tax purposes. That has been the situation. Government by its deliberate policy has supported that position, believing that Canada was well served and continued to be well served by foreign shipping.
In the last three or four years, and I am sure the minister is aware of this, the situation has changed. No longer arc the forces of shipping nearly as dependent upon market forces as they are on the forces and influence of government, in other words, political forces. That has changed the scene. From Mr. Howard Darling, we have a caution. We had signals that we should be changing our direction, that we must look at our sovereignty and that we must not act necessarily as other countries do, but we must act in our own best interests if we want to continue to enjoy the assurance of being able to move our goods.
The $3 billion to $4 billion that we now pay to foreign cartels is inexcusable. This situation should be turned around. We have the capacity in Canada. We have the trained seamen. Crew costs arc now no longer a major factor. 1 doubt if 10 per cent separates the highest paid and lowest paid crews of any flag in the western world. The cost of fuel oil has been the great reducing force. It has been the great leveller. All of these things brought together have created an atmosphere in which

countries, such as Canada, should move toward the development of their own fleets.
The former minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville, went very far in pursuing active conversations with the interested community and with Canadians generally. Had we carried on in government 1 am sure at this point in time we would have had before the Canadian public not only the framework within which to redevelop the Canadian presence on the oceans of the world, but we would have had a fair amount of meat on that framework.
Perhaps the minister could deal with the Cast situation and then give us some idea concerning a Canadian merchant marine. Perhaps he could tell us where these plans start. So that he will not think that I am after him too much and once we have seen on paper what is being proposed with respect to changes in the ports act, if there is nothing hidden in it and it is a straightforward attempt to correct a very serious situation, he will find that over here we are, most of the time, a co-operative and friendly group and we will be prepared to deal with it quite quickly.

Mr. Chairman, there are so many questions, one has a choice. The hon. member for Dartnrouth-Halifax East has mentioned Cast and the deep sea fleet. First, 1 might say with regard to Cast that CN acquired 18 per cent of that company in 1976. In July, CN moved to invest $7 million to maintain that 18 per cent position. Now, with the approval of cabinet, CN has invested $42 million in the project by way of preferred shares. These preferred shares can be converted at a later date-I do not remember the date exactly, but I think it is in 18 months. However, the decision has not been made. In the meantime, CN will have to answer a number of questions and explain to me, as Minister of Transport, and to my colleagues, the desirability of continuing or getting further into this project.
To conclude, the most recent decision does not affect the percentage ownership of CN in Cast. It does not prejudge either on this being or not being a contribution to the development of a deep sea fleet in Canada. In other words, it is a temporary situation. My colleague saw it as a good investment for CN, and I believe it is. The hon. member keeps saying that Cast is foreign owned. My information is that it is a Canadian company.
There is no doubt that the CN investment in Cast raises a number of questions as to CN's role. There are so many things that CN can do it is almost unbelievable. They have done a good number of these, one only being railway development. The company is into a deep sea fleet operation, port operation, ferry operation, and a great many others. Of course, there are some who say they should not go too far. Others, and I am one of them, see CN as being dynamic, aggressive, and forward moving. If there is a role for CN to play in the development of a deep sea fleet, why not? That is my position. As a Crown corporation, CN has a role in the development of government policy and consequently can be used as the avant-garde on a
number of moves. That is the way 1 see it, and I do not apologize for it.
On the subject of a deep sea fleet, 1 am delighted to know that my predecessor had a solution. I will gladly take it from him immediately after the House recesses. Seriously, the hon. member indicated there is a debate in Canada. It is a lively one. The disadvantage or the advantage, depending on where you stand, is that the free system as it now exists, to use a well-known phrase, has served the country well.
Some people see all kinds of dark clouds on the horizon in terms of government intervention, reduction of fleets of convenience in the world, with a cargo reservation between countries on a bilateral basis, the UNCTAD formula and so on. There are others who do not think that way, and they are still in the majority. Therefore, there is no agreement on what is ahead.
1 believe, along with my marine administrator, that we should be careful. We should try to hedge our bets. Consequently, the department and the minister have encouraged shipbuilders, ship owners and shippers to debate that subject extensively, and they are doing that. There have been a number of meetings with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Export Association to that effect. That is a condition sine qua non, as Shakespeare would say: if there is no agreement among the people interested in the subject, how could you impose a policy? Therefore we have encouraged a consensus development.

Mr. Chairman, I will answer as briefly as I can. Normally, I would not be giving precise answers to these questions because this is all before the committee. However, so much is already out that I can only confirm some of the news that has come out.
What is before the committee of the cabinet at this time is an approach, not a fully developed plan. This is being debated now in a friendly atmosphere, not in an atmosphere of confrontation as the press has suggested. I do not know where they get their facts. On top of that, they stated that I said it, when 1 said the opposite. In any event, the approach is now developing.
In simple terms, the approach is that the government would state a number of principles or beliefs, a number of things it holds to be true, as the Americans would say. It would then create a task force which would further explore the consensus which has developed in western Canada in recent years, particularly the western agricultural conference and the commodity coalition positions. They have a number of factors in common. We know what they are. There are other areas in which they have differences. The western agricultural conference, referring to the participation of farmers with regard to the freight rate, used the word "negotiate". I understood that to mean a desire to look at different possibilities. That would be the role of the task force. It would be under and would report to the Minister of Transport. On the basis of that report, in the hope that it will further the consensus, the
Supply
government would then announce the policies. The task force will be small in number, possibly three or five members.

Mr, Chairman, 1 will do my best. The hon. member is asking me for some very personal views. He said that he expressed his own views. He has more freedom where he sits now than I have as I sit here. Be that as it may, I think Senator Argue must have found comfort in the recommendation which was made at the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool the other day which, generally speaking, espoused the western agricultural conference approach and then, of course, took a fallback position which returned to the Crow. Senator Argue must have found satisfaction in that and, if he did, I will also.
Reference was made to an inquiry with respect to the CPR. Yes, indeed this was a resolution of the Liberal party at its last convention in Winnipeg. My views tend to go along with the views expressed by my hon. friend, that it would be difficult to carry the two enterprises in parallel line. However, it could be done. Some people would welcome that inquiry as having a cleansing effect on the reputation of the railway. I have heard that argument, but I personally hope-and I think this would be the approach-that an inquiry into the behaviour of CP would not influence the orientation or the progress toward Crow modernization.
On branch line rehabilitation, I remember that $240 million has been spent up to now and, as the hon. member knows, the total amount to be spent in the future under the program is $700 million over a period of eight years. That has not changed. A number of people say it might be a good idea to accelerate that program, and some in this regard, as in others, look with covetous eyes to the western development fund.
