subsubtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 2, 1980-81
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad of this opportunity to take part in the proceedings of the Committee of the Whole on the matter of transport, because I think the riding of Manicouagan can be readily identified with transport. In a sense, I am of the same mind as the Minister of Transport in that I do not know where to start, by Baie-Comeau, Blanc-Sablon, Schefferville, Fort-Chimo or Sept-fles, because if one considers the size of that riding, one readily realizes that transportation is not only a local but also a regional priority. It is with some emotion that 1 take part in this debate since a good friend of mine, who happens to be the mayor of Longue Pointe de Mingan and is also a pilot, has been missing for 48 hours. God be with him! But when talking about municipal airports or about means of transport in our country, one must take into account the human dimension of it all on top of the financial or administrative aspects because when it comes
down to it, all this technical equipment is there to help people. One realizes that it is important to have adequate equipment that works all year round when somebody is reported missing, like Mr. Leblanc.
First, 1 want to commend the Department of Transport for upgrading the airport facilities in some parts of my riding. I will deal later with some negative aspects but for now 1 want to underline the great improvements made to the Sept-Iles airport within the last three years. We now have quite a beautiful air terminal at a cost of $9.2 million. The same thing holds true for the equally modern Baie-Comeau airport which will benefit from some $4.5 million investments over the next five years. The same applies to the Natashquan airport which has now a paved runway; this may perhaps seem strange to hon. members, but I will just say that only a few weeks ago in a small community about 60 miles east of Natashquan, planes were landing on a runway lighted by oil lamps. The Natashquan runway is now paved, which is important locally since it allows landings and takeoffs regardless of frost and thaw.
The same holds true for the Gagnon airport where the Department of Transport is going to invest, as it was confirmed to me by the minister's office, over $4 million in the next two years, first of all to build an aircraft parking area because the people of Gagnon now have to walk 300 to 400 feet between the air terminal and the aircraft when often the runway is swept by strong northern winds. Those who have visited the place will find it is no luxury to have the aircraft come quite close to the air terminal. Because, when we board the plane at Gagnon, we really feel like refugees, we have to carry our luggage as best we can, and when we get off the plane, the situation is much the same.
All in all, things seem to be improving in the larger centres of the riding of Manicouagan, but in remote and isolated areas, they certainly are not. In that connection, 1 would not only ask the minister but also the officials who accompany him to listen with all their ears because I often have the feeling that 1 am crying in the wilderness and writing to God knows who, since the replies are often disappointing. I would even go further, Mr. Chairman. At times, I get the feeling that the civil servants are not always our allies, although I must say that we also have friends since we do get elected in our ridings by telling people the facts, whether we sit on one side of the House or the other; we arc still convinced that we know our areas quite well. And that is mainly why people elect us-to represent them.
When we have to consult senior officers from the Department of Transport we feel that we are facing a brick wall and that we are not dealing with people who are prepared to untangle the administrative jungle and plead our case. We feel that they put on the brakes not simply to slow us down but to bring us to a full stop. In that sense, it becomes very frustrating for members who have received a mandate from their
December 3, 1980

voters to find out that instead of working with allies they have to put up with systematic blocking.
And I can assure you that I know what I am talking about when I remember the file on the airport of Havre-Saint-Pierre, a ten-year old file. I do not want to accuse anyone, to put the blame on both sides; 1 do not intend to pass judgment on that but I think 1 spent more energy on that file than on all the other files of the constituency of Manicouagan put together. I had to phone. I figured out that I made 267 calls over a year and a half.
1 did the same thing with various ministers because at that time I had to call Mr. Mazankowski, Mr. Pepin and Mr. Lang and it is very difficult to feel the administrative and the political will. When you live in a remote part of the country, and I refer as well to constituencies such as Tcmiscamingue, Abitibi and Bonaventeure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, you really feel at times that you are alone in those battles. I understand that there is always the financial side, of course, but there is also a matter of priority, and this is where it fails apparently.
The question I will ask, because with 20 minutes one is very limited, is the one about the policy regarding small municipal airports. Some six months ago I requested a meeting with the minister. The minister was very polite and he told me that he had asked his officials to prepare a few scenarios before presenting them to the members who are always quite inquisitive.
The minister asked for a policy statement on municipal airports to be drafted in order for it to be tabled if possible before Christmas. I would like to ask especially of the department officials because they are those who are the closest advisers to the minister, if, at the level of their administration, there exists a distinction between those municipal airports which are, in my opinion, closer to the definition of flying clubs and those which are primarily municipally oriented airports such as Blanc-Sablon, Saint-Augustin, la Romaine, 1'Abitibi, Ungava Bay, James Bay, the Magdalen Islands. Are there truly established distinctions between the two types of airports?
In my area, between Havre-Saint-Pierre and Blanc-Sablon, there is a 400-mile stretch where there is no road. So when I raise the matter of municipal airports, I think in terms of mail, in terms of passenger service, of course, and in terms of transportation of patients and food supplies. So obviously we have no choice. The same thing applies in the case of the Magdalen Islands. There is no road between the islands and the mainland. For about a decade, we have been fighting over the kind of equipment necessary, over the type of aircraft. These days when men go to the moon and when we are contemplating with great emotion the rings of Saturn, I wonder how it can be possible that we should fail to solve such minor problems. I would not want to speak for the people in Sherbrooke or Drummondville, but surely a municipal airport in these areas is less important and deserves lower priority
Supply
than in areas like mine. Here is my question to the minister: what is being done for municipal airports, in terms of policy? I would like the officials to keep in mind that this is a priority for the people of our regions.
There is another important issue in the area of transport. I mean the maritime issue. We had in Baie-Comeau what was a rather special and, in my opinion, extremely simple problem, which was to discover the condition of the wharf before condemning it. DPW waited four months before making its report, after which DOT took some action. In the meantime, the Quebec government decided that repairs would cost $100,000 and they should go ahead as a priority without consulting the federal government. I believe it is about time jurisdictions were defined in such cases, and DOT should be able to make decisions more quickly without always having to wait for other departments. It should at least be able to put pressure on DPW to get it to act quickly. The wharf was condemned on June 6. I myself was in Baie-Comeau on the 7th, the report was ready on November 4, and the report had not been ordered before October. So what happened between June 6 and the early days of October? That is the question I ask and I would like to get an answer.
Another aspect in which I am deeply interested is the air transport rates. I would like to know from the minister whether there are special rate structures, that is, public assisted rates for areas in Canada or in Quebec other than Manicouagan. People living in Schefferville, Sept-Iles, Gagnon and Fairmour.t have no choice concerning transport. As I used to say, they arc living in the Siberia of Quebec or Canada, that is, they are quite isolated and they always have to travel by airplane.
Right now when we consider fuel prices and overhead costs which increase every day, I can understand why airline companies, in this instance Quebecair, have to raise their fares. What I cannot understand is why the department has not provided for a subsidy scheme or a tax credit for those users as they have no choice but to fly. 1 think that some other airline companies which link Newfoundland and the mainland get some public assistance. If a verification is not warranted in this case, what then can be done? I for one would prefer a tax credit formula which would go directly to the people, for if a company receives a direct grant the rates skyrocket after eight months or a year and then it is back to square one.
Therefore I think we should resolutely and officially study such cases and take strong action. And while I have the floor this afternoon I say that I wonder if anything will come out of this to show the strength of my belief, for I am often under the impression that we are talking to a wall when discussing such issues I wish that people listening everywhere in their offices and people who will read Hansard tomorrow would keep my questions in mind and come up with some answers. Nothing is worse than the lack of interest within the public administra-

December 3, 1980
Supply
tion. I often think that it is hon. members' daily lot, and I really wish that the civil servants would be aware of that and that the minister would follow up on this subject and even go beyond. I even wonder if the Department of Transport ought not to be divided in three sections so as to be really able to follow up on all these files. When we are speaking of transport, we are speaking of air, sea and land transport, and it is very hard for one man to be aware of every aspect of the issue. I therefore believe that for effectiveness we should perhaps consider splitting the department and creating several ministries under the direction of a titular minister to be sure that some progress is being made.
I have had the opportunity to travel throughout Canada with the transport committee in the company of my colleague opposite from Regina East and other members, and we saw for ourselves that there are many problems. People often complain, not necessarily about identifying a problem, but about the time it takes after a problem is found to exist and before action is taken or even before an answer is received.
These are facts that we have been able to verify during the first two weeks of September, and everywhere in Canada we realize that the lapse of time between the moment when a problem is identified and the moment when action is taken is such that very often the problem has changed considerably. 1 therefore believe that the minister should perhaps review the operational methods of his department. I am not in any position to tell him what to do in this area, but it is my view that people for whom transportation is a daily experience, and to me in my area it is all in a day's work, those people feel that the department must be reorganized to become more efficient, with a higher degree of delegation to the regional level. 1 for one have to be called almost every day for 15 days at freeze-up time, because in my area aircraft cannot land on the lakes, for lack of ice. The plane does not stop, there are no roads and no water transportation services.
We have the same problem during the spring, there is a three-week thaw period on a 400-mile coastline, with a population of 5,000. Airplanes cannot land because we have no instruments, no equipment. At that time people call us to complain there has been no crossing for three or four days, and sick people have to be moved out. This requires helicopter services, but we are not authorized to order helicopter transportation. These are everyday problems in an area like Mani-couagan. When we write or speak about this, it has a frontier, a folklore flair. Well, to us it is unacceptable. I realize the Manicouagan district may be the most expensive, per capita, to the Department of Transport.
I can understand that but is it a valid reason to leave things as they are? I admit that there has been much progress in the past 20 years, but not enough. And even more, I notice works that are being done in the constituency which are perhaps less necessary, which are even luxurious, but some cuts could be made in some places to give elsewhere. I do not ask for more
funds in the constituency but I ask that the investments be more judicious and I will give you a specific example. A parking lot is now being built in Baie-Comeau at a cost of $350,000 yet not more than 40 cars use it in a week. Is it necessary? I doubt it.
With the kind of equipment installed at Sept-Iles, one has to pay 50 cents to park for a full day when next door it actually costs 75 cents an hour. Imagine! And they advertise that to boot. It costs 50 cents to park a whole day yet the other lot next door charges 75 cents an hour. You see what 1 mean. That is what we get from the Department of Transport. One has to take a ticket. If you are about to board a plane and you do not have 50 cents to put in the slot to get a ticket, you have to go through the airport.
It is forbidden to park in front of it, and you have a bill so you then have to get some change and come back to park with your 50 cents. No one is bright enough to put someone in the little box at the back who could at least make change. It is all those things that make administration absolutely flabbergasting; I wonder why we are not consulted about things like that because 1 claim to know my riding better than some people.
I can understand that things have to be done like that in Montreal or Quebec City where parking has to be better controlled, but in places like back home, those things cost a fortune. It is a matter of deciding what should be uniform in public administration and what special measures can be allowed from time to time. That is what I would like to see the civil servants of the department look into.
Of course, I understand that the minister should be put on the spot because he is not aware of all those problems. The primary function of department officials is to give advice but, good grief, one has to know the place to be able to do so. That is my bone of contention. Frustration becomes so bad that we have it up to here. There comes a time when we are getting really impatient and when we want action. I for one intend to keep after the Department of Transport because it is vitally important to us. Of course, when you go to the doctor's you do not tell him what is right, so what is happening this afternoon is about the same. I point out more often what is wrong, but we should admit that certain things are right. I have to commend the minister and the National Harbours Board for putting $45 million to $50 million in the national harbour of Sept-Iles over the next three years. This is fundamental.
I should also commend the minister for the decision he made at last, after ten years, authorizing the airport of Havre-Saint-Pierre, and I should like to ask him in the same breath whether he intends to confirm the regional vocation of that airport. Recently 1 asked that question in committee. I was told that the situation was being re-examined. Quebecair has applied for landing rights in Havre-Saint-Pierre and the company Fer et Titane which has some facilities in Havre-Saint-Pierre would like to expand there, and I think we have all the elements to make a decision. If you make other types of decisions regard-
December 3, 1980

ing this issue then I think it will be against the public interest and against regional and local interests in this area. That is an important dimension of this issue.
I would have many other things to add. I would have liked to speak about Ungava Bay, James Bay, Fort Chimo, Sugluk and some other communities. Maybe we can come back on the subject at a later time. Perhaps 1 should let the minister answer. 1 know that this is a broad subject, that time is limited but I think that our people are becoming restless and the time has now come to act.

May I say the following, for the record. [Translation]
I listened with a great deal of pleasure of course to the impassionated speech by the hon. member for Manicouagan who spoke of the individual member's frustrations, and I understand that, i must add, however, that in the two examples he gave he won his case. Fie forgot to mention it for both Havre-Saint-Pierre and Baie-Comeau. Fie at least got part of what he wanted, which shows that time and patience are more productive than strength and frenzy. But I sympathize with this and if I had more time 1 would speak of the frustrations of ministers and public servants. Despite the impression to the contrary that ministers and public servants may sometimes give, we also suffer from not being able to grant all requests made to us, especially when they are justified as in so many cases.
I also want to say that there is a sense of frustration, but I am not going to whine on the floor of the House, on the part of public servants and ministers, and it is annoying for anybody not to be able to please everyone.
Finally, it is a question of dollars. My department had a small airport aid program of limited scope. It had $3 million, which was taken away before I arrived, so 1 cannot accept responsibility for what was done before my time, no doubt for very good reasons. That was what the restraint program required at that time. We could theorize at length on the priority concept. What is a priority? A very nice phrase from the hon. member. There are less necessary things that some view as luxuries and necessities to others, and some necessary things that appear as luxuries. That could lead to a philosophic discourse on the concept of luxury and the concept of the necessary. We all know very well that what was a luxury yesterday could be necessary today. That also applies to us, as members of Parliament. 1 am doing everything I can to revive that small assistance program for small airports to provide for the cases the hon. member has referred to, but as a rule my department-and I say so without affectation-has suffered greatly in the area of investments for airports and equipment. The figures will tell you that five or six years ago the budget
Supply
was around $250 million. It is now down to $85 million or $95 million. Obviously all that shows, and the result is that fewer good causes can be accommodated.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to talk about the progress the government has made to date on the transportation of hazardous goods. I think it is an appropriate thing for a member from Mississauga to do, a year after the famous Mississauga derailment.
On the anniversary date of the derailment a conference took place in Toronto which attracted international experts and produced a lot of opinions about the government's progress so far. One person who was sharply critical of the federal government and its standards a year ago was the mayor of Mississauga. Subsequently I spoke with her about the government's progress over the past year, and I think 1 can fairly say that some genuine progress has been made of which we now can be proud. I should like the minister to give us a progress report on this matter, because as I travel around Mississauga I am asked regularly whether in fact a similar accident can be prevented.
I have served on the transport committee and had the pleasure of working on the two bills passed last spring. The first bill brought container standards up to international levels, and the second and more famous one dealt with the domestic transportation of hazardous goods.
Linder the second law we were able to bring about standards which affect both accident prevention and accident reaction. In that law we allowed for the provision of regulations which will enforce safe standards for designing containers, packages, and moving equipment. We require proper labelling and handling so that ordinary people who must deal with these goods will know what is going on and not only how to react after an accident but how to prevent one. Also in this bill there is a provision for inspections to ensure the standards we set actually stick. The labelling and inspection powers we have set out will also help us-and this was a crucial point raised at the conference; undoubtedly it will be a point which Mr. Justice Samuel Grange will discuss-to react properly after an accident, as well as to prevent an accident ahead of time.

December 3, 1980
Supply
The work we undertook in the spring was in order to give the government the power, capacity or authority to do it. It does not necessarily mean that the government will have the will-power or the desire to do it, but I was heartened by the progress of the Department of Transport. Indeed it is an indication that the department has the will-power and desire to prevent future derailments like the one at Mississauga.
1 should like to refer to an article which appeared in The Financial Post dated November 29, in which an unidentified federal official said the following:
"The act provides for the setting of safety standards for the equipping of a means of transport. If we feel that a certain regulatory agency is slow to regulate standards ... we can write them into our regulations. We may be stepping on a few toes, but it has to be done."
Comments such as those indicate a real desire to go ahead and get the job done, and not just to put a lot of cosmetic legislation into place.
If I ask the minister to reply now, his report will be very short because of the remaining time. I wonder if I might leave with him until tomorrow the idea that 1 should like a comment on the progress. I should like him to comment on his negotiations with the provinces and his review of his own regulations. 1 should like him to take a look at the ways he has beefed up his inspection standards and personnel. I should like to know something about his budget commitments. Perhaps he can tell us about the sources of information which will be set up for individual communities so that they have access to information to help prevent accidents and to react to accidents. By setting the law in place we in fact indicated we were very serious about this question and that we were not going through simple cosmetic procedures. 1 hope the minister will give us the details which will inspire some confidence in the people in my area, so that they will know another accident like this is not likely to happen.
In view of the fact that it would be logical to break my discussion at this point, may I call it six o'clock?
